newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major says failed EMU would crack open Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major says failed EMU would crack open Europe.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major told the annual Conservative Party conference on Wednesday that if a single European currency failed it would "crack wide open the European Union".

Major was speaking in a question and answer session with Conservative party members. Major was asked whether it was true that Britain would lose its influence in Europe if it ruled out a participation in a single currency now.

He told one member asking about rising pension liabilities in Europe: "You illustrate one of the reasons precisely...why the British government needs to be in the negotiations to make sure the convergence criteria are appropriate."

Answering another questioner, he said: "If a single currency goes ahead it will have an impact in one way or another on every nation in the European Union, whether or not that country is in the single currency...
"If it fails... then the fall-out from failed economic and monetary union would make the fall-out from the failed (European) exchange rate mechanism look like a teddy-bears' picnic," Major said.

Britain would continue to take part in discussions over a European currency to ensure that the conditions for those countries entering conformed with the convergence criteria agreed in the Maastricht Treaty.
"This is an issue that if it were to go wrong would crack wide open the European Union... If it cracked it would impact on this country as well... so we need to have our voice."
Major confirmed that a Conservative government would hold a referendum if it decided to join a single currency.
But he took the opportunity to attack bitter infighting in the Conservatives over the single currency, saying it was handicapping the ruling party's efforts to defeat Labour.

He said the differences between Labour and the Conservatives on Europe would become clear "if this party stopped conducting an internal debate with itself and started conducting a debate with the electorate and the Labour party."
